newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine bans grain movement, says only temporary.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine bans grain movement, says only temporary.

text.p: Ukraine, in a move which infuriated the agricultural sector and countries paying to reform it, has taken control of much of the grain harvest until state needs are met.
But a spokesman for newly-appointed Agriculture Minister Yuri Karasyk said the ban was under review and had been instigated by Pavlo Lazarenko, sacked as prime minister in July.
"We take a negative view of it," he said.

Like last year when exchanges ground to a halt and brokers begged the government to release pre-purchased grain, the wheat, barley and maize in state-owned elevators and farms has been on hold for at least two weeks.
Independent grain sources were hoping for a reprieve from the ban, which went against reform principles Ukraine has repeatedly promised its investors it will adopt.

"It's in many ways wider than it was last year," said Peter Sochan, senior policy coordinator at Citizens' Network, a U.S.-funded group set up to promote private business in Ukraine's largely state-controlled agricultural sector.

"The sense is that it's country-wide. The indication is that the initial direction is coming down from the central government," Sochan said, adding either verbal or written bans had been issued in at least half Ukraine's 26 regions.
He said the government was pressuring collective farms to pay back years of accumulated debt -- preferably in grain.

Grain brokers and local and foreign companies said they are still reeling from last year's unofficial ban, since without a written government order as evidence of force majeure many were liable for breach of contract.

Roger Wolfe said his U.S. firm Global Ag Management stood to lose $100,000 in grain it tried to collect for debts from 1996. "There was a state order saying that until the order is fulfilled, no other persons get grain from the harvest".

Ukrainian officials like Serhiy Tyhypko, deputy prime minister of reforms, have said the grain movement ban would not happen again -- though the government never formally admitted to issuing last year's order.

But there were signs that Washington, which put Ukraine third in line for aid after Israel and Egypt, was annoyed. In a July 30 letter obtained by Reuters U.S. Ambassador William Miller requested a meeting with Tyhypko and hinted Ukraine's foreign funding could be endangered.
"The preferential acquisition of grain and other products... means that the Ukrainian government will control or own the majority of the 1997 harvest," the letter said.
It recalled how President Leonid Kuchma had promised the U.S. that Ukraine, due to receive $225 million in the 1998 fiscal year, would guarantee the free movement of grain.
The U.S. has said it would deliver only half the aid until Ukraine proved it was reforming economically and fighting widespread corruption.
Ukraine, once the breadbasket of the Soviet Union, has forecast a grain harvest of 37-38 million tonnes this year against last year's drought-hit crop of 25.4 million tonnes.
The state order, set to be cancelled in 1998, stands at 5.88 million tonnes compared to 5.0 million tonnes last year.
